questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a minimum viable product in this chapter?
choices: To complete one build-measure-learn cycle with minimum waste
To release the cheapest version possible
To impress investors with speed

explanation.gentle: Ries defines MVP by the learning cycle it completes, not by cheapness alone.
explanation.direct: The chapter says an MVP exists to learn with minimum waste.
explanation.competitive: Its job is to close one honest loop, not to win a race to the bottom.

questions.prompt: Why is an MVP not the same as simply building something cheap?
choices: Because cheap products are always high quality
Because minimal is defined by the learning goal, not by low effort alone
Because MVPs are only used after launch

explanation.gentle: The product has to be big enough to test the important assumption honestly.
explanation.direct: Minimal is relative to what the team needs to learn, not to a generic wish to do less.
explanation.competitive: Cheap is useless if it cannot force the belief to answer.

questions.prompt: A team wants to learn whether users will request a service, but it has not built automation yet. What fits Chapter 6 best?
choices: Wait until the full system is built
Use a manual or concierge version if it can reveal real behavior
Skip testing and rely on interviews alone

explanation.gentle: Manual delivery can count if it still teaches whether users value the service enough to act.
explanation.direct: The chapter allows concierge forms when they complete the learning cycle around the key assumption.
explanation.competitive: Let humans do the work first if that is the fastest honest way to make demand answer.

questions.prompt: In Devin's postmortem, what made the so-called MVP a problem?
choices: It was too manual
It was too polished before the team learned whether users cared
It was tested in a work setting

explanation.gentle: The team spent heavily before completing the learning cycle the MVP was supposed to enable.
explanation.direct: The product became polished while the core value question stayed open.
explanation.competitive: The team overbuilt a question mark and called it progress.

choices: Only as poor code quality
As any effort spent before the key assumption has earned that effort through learning
As any product that uses manual labor

explanation.gentle: Waste includes work done before the business knows whether the assumption deserves more investment.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats premature build effort as waste when proof is still missing.
explanation.competitive: Build work that outruns evidence is just expensive guessing.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures why low-fidelity or concierge MVPs can be valid?
choices: They always save the most money
They are easier to market than polished products
They can reveal the right user behavior without premature overbuilding

explanation.gentle: The form is valid when it still teaches what the business needs to know.
explanation.direct: Rough or manual formats count if they expose the assumption honestly and quickly.
explanation.competitive: If the rough form gets the truth faster, glamor loses the argument.

questions.prompt: How could a school or nonprofit team misuse the MVP idea?
choices: By making the test so thin that it gets comments but not the real behavior the project depends on
By using volunteers to deliver the first version
By testing assumptions before building a full system

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that smaller is not better if the real assumption never gets tested.
explanation.direct: A too-thin MVP can create reactions while missing the behavior that matters.
explanation.competitive: Lean turns fake when the product is small enough to dodge the truth.

questions.prompt: What does Chapter 6 say about a polished build completed before the first real learning cycle?
choices: It may be wasteful if the key assumption is still untested
It is always the ideal MVP
It proves that the business is ready to scale

explanation.gentle: Polish does not justify itself if the important assumption still lacks evidence.
explanation.direct: A polished first release can be waste when the business has not earned that effort through learning.

questions.prompt: When does making an MVP smaller become a problem?
choices: When the team can no longer release it publicly
When the MVP no longer tests the important assumption honestly
When the prototype uses manual delivery

explanation.gentle: The chapter's hard question is how far the team can shrink the test before it loses the lesson.
explanation.direct: Smaller becomes harmful when it weakens the truth of the evidence instead of merely reducing waste.
explanation.competitive: Too small is the moment efficient starts meaning evasive.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 6 connect to Chapter 7?
choices: Chapter 7 abandons measurement and focuses only on motivation
Chapter 7 asks how the startup measures what the MVP actually proved
Chapter 7 argues that all MVPs should become polished products immediately

explanation.gentle: After running the MVP, the team needs a way to judge what was really learned.
explanation.direct: The chapter points toward innovation accounting and stronger measurement.
explanation.competitive: Once the rough test lands, the next demand is honest scorekeeping.
